sources.entry: Celebrate tiny learning milestones, Julia Evans.

summary.title: Celebrate tiny learning milestones
summary.one_liner: Track programming progress with small, frequent "milestones" you can celebrate, instead of big goals that feel like failures when missed.
takeaways: Goals set years ago can feel stressful and unhelpful; reframing progress as tiny milestones makes it easier to see growth.
A milestone is a small marker of progress, such as using a new tool, fixing a new kind of bug, or learning a new concept.
Fixing a bug you could not fix before counts as a milestone; the author dug into a flexbox bug rather than applying a workaround.
Changing goals is healthy when your original goal no longer has a real reason behind it; skills like strace, gdb, and Rust were learned instead.
Celebrate milestones by writing blog posts or recording them in a brag document.
summary.summary: The author, Julia Evans, argues that programming goals can be stressful and unhelpful, using her own nine-year-old goals to learn C and C++ as an example that went unmet. She proposes tracking tiny milestones instead, such as learning strace, gdb, ELF layout, or static versus dynamic linking, each of which took under a week. The post shows how many systems skills came up naturally through projects and bugs, and it recommends celebrating these milestones through blog posts or a brag document. It is a personal essay with no code or tutorial steps.
